bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Long-standing association with Jindal Pipes Limited: the company sells all its finished product under the 'Jindal Star' brand to JPL and its approved customers on monthly card rates, with JPL facilitating entire procurement and selling, which the company says makes pricing transparent and makes pass-through of raw-material price variation effective
- Access to JPL's distribution and marketing network, which the company says extends customer reach and shortens delivery turnaround
- Strategic plant locations: Raigad for export logistics (100% of exports shipped from Unit I), Mahabubnagar near Hyderabad and the Jadcherla industrial area for logistics, power, water and raw-material access, and Sundergarh near eastern raw-material sources and markets
- First-generation promoter-led company: promoters Mr. Vijay Kaushik and Mr. Vibhor Kaushik have over 4 and 2 decades of individual experience respectively in the steel pipes and tubes industry
- Quality accreditations (ISO, BIS, TUV, ISI) plus 100% Eddy Current and hydro-testing of end products, supporting sales into both domestic and international markets
- Diversified product portfolio spanning commodity GI/ERW pipes through to higher-value crash barriers, transmission towers and poles, with sizes and specifications from 20 Nb to 100 Nb
- Raw material (hot rolled coils) sourced from established suppliers including SAIL and JSW
- Counterpoint the company states about itself: its brand development is at a relatively nascent stage versus peers with on average 40 years' longer operating history, and it intends to strengthen goodwill with the help of Jindal Pipes Limited
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Customer and channel concentration in Jindal Pipes Limited — Not listed by management among its named risks, but structurally the largest one disclosed: under a business agreement renewed April 01, 2023 the Company sells all its finished product under the 'Jindal Star' brand to JPL and its approved customers on monthly card rates, with JPL facilitating entire procurement and selling, and JPL also underpinning the distribution and marketing network and brand goodwill. Loss or renegotiation of that arrangement would affect both the sales channel and the raw-material sourcing channel simultaneously. Read in the MD&A business-strengths section of the profile bundle (cross-bundle).
- Input / raw material price risk — Management states raw materials form a significant cost component and volatility in key raw material prices has a significant bearing on earnings, while limited availability or unavailability of any raw material may hamper the production process. Mitigation cited: diversified raw-material sources geographically and by vendor, buffer inventory, long-term supplier contracts and close monitoring of stock levels. The Chairman separately attributes FY26 margin pressure to volatility in steel prices and fluctuations in input costs.
- Supply-demand risk from oversupply and low-cost imports — Management states that in the event of oversupply or overcapacity there will be a rise in low-cost imports into India, so steel prices may fall and impact indigenous players. The MD&A industry review reinforces this: Chinese steel exports exceeded 110 million tonnes, the highest in nearly a decade, intensifying international competition and prompting anti-dumping investigations, and India faces increased imports from China and other Asian countries.
- Economic / cyclical demand risk — Management states steel-sector demand is highly dependent on steel-consuming sectors such as oil and gas, construction, capital goods, consumer durables and autos, so an economic downturn will have a strong bearing on steel demand. Mitigation cited: geographical diversification, brand equity and a broad range of products across end-user sectors.
- Competition risk — Management states that given the growth prospects of the steel industry the Company faces intense competition from existing players and new entrants, and that any change in competitors' marketing strategies or the introduction of superior technology may intensify competition. The Company also acknowledges its brand development is at a relatively nascent stage against peers with on average 40 years' longer operating history.
- Regulatory and environmental compliance risk — Management states the global steel industry is highly regulated and failure to comply with an existing or new regulation may impact the normal course of business. This risk crystallised during the year: the Secretarial Audit Report records that the Telangana State Pollution Control Board issued an unconditional claim letter to HDFC Bank forfeiting a bank guarantee for non-compliance with the Water Act 1974 and Air Act 1981 — acid spillage, furnace-oil spillage, storing untreated effluents, no hazardous-waste storage shed and sludge stored openly in bags. Cross-bundle: the Secretarial Audit content arrives in the profile bundle.
- Foreign exchange risk — Management states the Company has foreign-currency exposure from trading raw materials and finished goods across international geographies plus additional payments in foreign currency, and that volatility in forex rates impacts earnings. Mitigation cited: an FX risk management system, hedging of the forex position and use of derivative instruments including forward contracts. Material to watch given the stated intent to scale exports 10x over five years from 3%-5% of revenue.
- Execution and financing risk on the Odisha expansion — The new Sundergarh (Odisha) unit was debt-funded, and management attributes the FY26 fall in profitability to higher depreciation from commissioning the facility and higher finance costs from borrowings availed for the expansion project. The return on the expansion is contingent on the plant reaching optimal capacity utilisation; until then the fixed-cost and interest burden weighs on earnings. The Company also wrote off a capital advance paid to Punjab National Bank, Sambalpur in connection with a proposed e-auction property acquisition in Odisha that was deemed no longer recoverable.

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers

business.body: Established in 2003, VSTL manufactures and distributes steel pipes and tubes and value-added steel infrastructure products from three plants in Raigad (Maharashtra), Mahabubnagar (Telangana) and Sundergarh (Odisha), plus a warehouse in Hisar, Haryana. Its products serve infrastructure, construction, power transmission, transportation, oil & gas, water distribution, agriculture, telecommunications and heavy engineering customers in India and abroad. The company sells its finished product under the brand name 'Jindal Star' to Jindal Pipes Limited and its approved customers under a business agreement renewed on April 01, 2023, with JPL facilitating both procurement and selling.

- **Infrastructure / value-added steel products:** Crash barriers, Transmission line towers, High mast lighting poles, Octagonal poles, Monopoles

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Consolidate and ramp up the newly commissioned Unit III at Sundergarh, Odisha (156,000 MTPA), improving capacity utilisation so that operating leverage, lower logistics costs and improved efficiencies flow through to profitability in coming years.
- Shift the product mix towards value-added infrastructure products — crash barriers, octagonal poles, high mast lighting poles and transmission line towers — which management identifies as the margin-accretive segments, moving the GI-pipes-to-others mix from 90:10 to 75:25 by FY28.
- Expand the international footprint: scale exports (currently 3%-5% of revenue) by 10x over the next five years, selecting new geographies where quality products can be delivered without significant delays, and using geographic diversification as a hedge against concentration in limited areas.
- Deepen the Jindal Pipes Limited relationship, which management says provides stability and business visibility, and use JPL's distribution and marketing network and dealer meets to strengthen VSTL's own goodwill and brand recall towards parity with longer-established peers.
- Improve operating efficiencies through technology enhancement — further develop technology systems in line with proposed expansion plans to increase asset productivity and strengthen competitive position.
- Attract, retain and train qualified engineering and technical personnel, with continuous training in latest systems and techniques, as the basis for execution quality, cost control and timely completion.
- Prudent capital allocation and disciplined execution — the Board retained FY26 profits rather than paying a dividend, in order to meet the requirements of future growth.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The defining expansion event of FY 2025-26 was the commissioning of Unit III at Sundergarh, Odisha. The unit started manufacturing in June 2025, is situated on over 23.98 acres about 20 km from Sundergarh city, and was built at a stated investment of 119.83 crores. It manufactures pipes, transmission towers, crash barriers, octagonal poles and high mast lighting poles, and carries a manufacturing capacity of 156,000 MTPA — larger than either of the two existing units (Raigad, Maharashtra at 125,000 MTPA and Mahabubnagar, Telangana at 96,000 MTPA), taking the group total to the 377,000 MT annual production capacity cited in the At a Glance spread. The Chairman describes FY26 as a year of consolidation and ramp-up of the expanded Odisha capability, which strengthens the geographical presence in eastern India and broadens the product portfolio into infrastructure products. Management states the plant is located close to major raw material sources and key markets, and expects operating leverage, optimised raw-material sourcing, lower logistics costs and greater economies of scale as utilisation improves. The expansion was debt-funded — the Directors' Report attributes the increase in finance costs to borrowings availed for funding the expansion project, and the rise in depreciation to the commissioning of the Odisha facility. The milestone timeline also records earlier capacity steps: commencement at 25,000 MTPA at Unit-I, enhancement to 60,000 MTPA, then 90,000 MTPA with machinery from Australia and the USA, establishment of Unit-II in Telangana at 96,000 MTPA, commissioning of a 12-inch tube mill, doubling of Telangana GI capacity to 48,000 MTPA, and addition of a warehouse at Hisar, Haryana. Subsequent to the year end, on 17 June 2026, the company incorporated a wholly owned subsidiary, Viyom Steel Infra Private Limited, in Hisar, Haryana, to diversify into manufacturing of infrastructure-related products including transmission towers, monopoles, crash barriers, octagonal poles, high mast poles and pre-fab structures (read in the governance_entities and registry bundles, Directors' Report item 20 — cross-bundle sourcing). No further named capex project with a commissioning timeline is disclosed for FY27 onwards; the Board states only a general commitment to expanding capacities.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Government infrastructure spending is the primary stated demand driver: the Union Budget 2025-26 allocated capital expenditure of INR 11.21 lakh crore towards infrastructure, and programmes named include the National Infrastructure Pipeline, PM Gati Shakti, Jal Jeevan Mission, Smart Cities Mission, Bharatmala, railway modernisation, PMAY Urban 2.0 and Gramin, and city gas distribution network expansion.
- Management expects domestic steel demand in India to grow by approximately 8-9% during FY 2026-27, significantly outpacing global demand growth, with India remaining the fastest-growing major steel market.
- Global steel demand is projected to grow by approximately 1.0%-1.5% during 2026 to around 1.77 billion tonnes, per the MD&A industry outlook.
- Third-party market sizing cited by management: the global steel pipes and tubes market at approximately USD 137.6 billion in 2025 projected to USD 209.9 billion by 2033 at a 6.0% CAGR (Grand View Research), with Asia-Pacific over 60% of the global market; and the Indian steel pipes and tubes market at approximately USD 31.6 billion in 2025 expected to reach around USD 47.8 billion by 2030 at approximately 8.6% CAGR.
- Company-specific margin lever: the Odisha plant is located close to major raw material sources and key markets, so as it reaches optimal capacity utilisation management expects operating leverage, optimised raw material sourcing, reduced logistics costs and greater economies of scale to improve margins and profitability.
- Near-term margin headwind management flags: volatility in steel prices and fluctuations in input costs impacted margins during FY26, and the Odisha expansion raised depreciation and finance costs during the initial phase of operations.
- Sector headwinds management flags: excess global steelmaking capacity, elevated Chinese steel exports (exceeding 110 million tonnes, the highest in nearly a decade) intensifying international competition and prompting anti-dumping investigations, rising protectionist trade measures, and increased low-cost imports into India from China and other Asian countries.
- End-market demand for the specific product set is expected to be supported by government focus on infrastructure, manufacturing growth, housing, transportation, power transmission, water distribution and industrial expansion — the exact applications of the company's pipes, crash barriers and transmission towers.
- The macro backdrop management cites for FY 2026-27: India GDP growth projected at 6.8% with agriculture, industry and services growing 3.7%, 6.6% and 7.4% respectively, and inflation contained at around 4.1%.
- The transition to low-carbon steel production is expected to accelerate globally (EAF, hydrogen-based DRI), with the Ministry of Steel allocated INR 455 crore under the National Green Hydrogen Mission for hydrogen-steelmaking pilots — noted by management as an industry-level trend rather than a company programme.
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Vibhor Steel is transitioning from a pure-play pipe manufacturer to a diversified infrastructure component supplier with the commissioning of its Odisha plant, targeting a 75:25 mix shift toward higher-margin products like transmission towers and crash barriers. Immediate earnings are buoyed by a ~Rs 3,000/ton steel price rally on large inventory holdings, while long-term value lies in pending Power Grid approvals unlocking the transmission tower segment.

risks.note: Not listed by management among its named risks, but structurally the largest one disclosed: under a business agreement renewed April 01, 2023 the Company sells all its finished product under the 'Jindal Star' brand to JPL and its approved customers on monthly card rates, with JPL facilitating entire procurement and selling, and JPL also underpinning the distribution and marketing network and brand goodwill. Loss or renegotiation of that arrangement would affect both the sales channel and the raw-material sourcing channel simultaneously. Read in the MD&A business-strengths section of the profile bundle (cross-bundle).
risks.risk: Customer and channel concentration in Jindal Pipes Limited

risks.note: Management states raw materials form a significant cost component and volatility in key raw material prices has a significant bearing on earnings, while limited availability or unavailability of any raw material may hamper the production process. Mitigation cited: diversified raw-material sources geographically and by vendor, buffer inventory, long-term supplier contracts and close monitoring of stock levels. The Chairman separately attributes FY26 margin pressure to volatility in steel prices and fluctuations in input costs.

Management states that in the event of oversupply or overcapacity there will be a rise in low-cost imports into India, so steel prices may fall and impact indigenous players. The MD&A industry review reinforces this: Chinese steel exports exceeded 110 million tonnes, the highest in nearly a decade, intensifying international competition and prompting anti-dumping investigations, and India faces increased imports from China and other Asian countries.
risks.risk: Supply-demand risk from oversupply and low-cost imports

risks.note: Management states steel-sector demand is highly dependent on steel-consuming sectors such as oil and gas, construction, capital goods, consumer durables and autos, so an economic downturn will have a strong bearing on steel demand. Mitigation cited: geographical diversification, brand equity and a broad range of products across end-user sectors.

Management states that given the growth prospects of the steel industry the Company faces intense competition from existing players and new entrants, and that any change in competitors' marketing strategies or the introduction of superior technology may intensify competition. The Company also acknowledges its brand development is at a relatively nascent stage against peers with on average 40 years' longer operating history.

Management states the global steel industry is highly regulated and failure to comply with an existing or new regulation may impact the normal course of business. This risk crystallised during the year: the Secretarial Audit Report records that the Telangana State Pollution Control Board issued an unconditional claim letter to HDFC Bank forfeiting a bank guarantee for non-compliance with the Water Act 1974 and Air Act 1981 — acid spillage, furnace-oil spillage, storing untreated effluents, no hazardous-waste storage shed and sludge stored openly in bags. Cross-bundle: the Secretarial Audit content arrives in the profile bundle.

Management states the Company has foreign-currency exposure from trading raw materials and finished goods across international geographies plus additional payments in foreign currency, and that volatility in forex rates impacts earnings. Mitigation cited: an FX risk management system, hedging of the forex position and use of derivative instruments including forward contracts. Material to watch given the stated intent to scale exports 10x over five years from 3%-5% of revenue.

The new Sundergarh (Odisha) unit was debt-funded, and management attributes the FY26 fall in profitability to higher depreciation from commissioning the facility and higher finance costs from borrowings availed for the expansion project. The return on the expansion is contingent on the plant reaching optimal capacity utilisation; until then the fixed-cost and interest burden weighs on earnings. The Company also wrote off a capital advance paid to Punjab National Bank, Sambalpur in connection with a proposed e-auction property acquisition in Odisha that was deemed no longer recoverable.
risks.risk: Execution and financing risk on the Odisha expansion
